meta.title: Who really said "I'm not concerned with your liking or disliking me. All I ask is that you respect me as a human being"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Real Jackie Robinson. He said it to an umpire on a 1954 flight and printed it himself in Baseball Has Done It (1964) — not to teammates in 1947.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'm not concerned with your liking or disliking me. All I ask is that you respect me as a human being'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Robinson's 1954 reply to an umpire, printed in his own 1964 book Baseball Has Done It. The famous two sentences are genuine, just truncated.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1919–1972 · Brooklyn Dodgers infielder & civil rights advocate
answer.sourceLine: Robinson said it in 1954 on a plane, to a baseball umpire who had known him since his 1946 minor-league season and who had just told him, “I liked you much better when you were less aggressive.” He printed the exchange himself in Baseball Has Done It (Lippincott, 1964) — the two famous sentences open a much longer answer that ends “I am not an Uncle Tom. I am in this fight to stay.”

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Lippincott, Philadelphia, 1964; edited by Charles Dexter; 216 pp.
A 1954 plane conversation with an umpire who had known Robinson since 1946

source.excerpt:
“What’s made you change your attitude, Jackie? I liked you much better when you were less aggressive.”

“I’m not concerned with your liking or disliking me. All I ask is that you respect me as a human being. I am not ashamed of my dark skin. You and every other white American should understand that we believe our color is an asset. Your dislike of my aggressiveness has no effect on me. I’m after something much more important than your favor or disfavor. You should at least admit that you respect me as a man who stands up for what he believes in. I am not an Uncle Tom. I am in this fight to stay.”
trail: English Wikiquote ↗ carries the full passage in its sourced Quotes section, with the note that Robinson was “Responding, circa 1954, to an umpire who had known him 8 years before… as quoted in Baseball Has Done It (1964) by Robinson, pp. 9–10.”

The Harvard Crimson’s 1972 tribute ↗ reproduces the exchange in full and supplies the setting: “Jackie Robinson boarded a plane with an umpire who had known him since 1946 when Robinson was a rookie in the International League.”

Open Library’s search-inside index ↗ returns the paragraph from inside two scanned copies of Baseball has done it by Jackie Robinson, confirming the book itself contains the wording rather than only later quote books.
The Open Library edition record ↗ gives the bibliographic detail: Lippincott, Philadelphia, 1964, 216 pages, “by Jackie Robinson; edited by Charles Dexter.”
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from The Harvard Crimson’s 1972 reprint of the exchange ↗. Wikiquote’s text of the same passage ↗ reads “You should at least respect me as a man…” where the Crimson has “at least admit that you respect me…” The two famous opening sentences are identical in both.

author.name: Jackie Robinson
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: 1919–1972 · Brooklyn Dodgers, 1947–1956 · Baseball Hall of Fame, 1962
author.bio: Jack Roosevelt Robinson broke Major League Baseball’s color line with the Brooklyn Dodgers, played his whole big-league career in Brooklyn from 1947 to 1956, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1962. For his first three seasons he kept a promise to Dodgers general manager Branch Rickey not to fight back; once Rickey told him — in the Crimson’s account — “You’ve earned the right to be yourself, Jackie,” he became one of the most outspoken Black public figures in America. That change is exactly what the umpire on the 1954 flight was complaining about, and exactly what Robinson refused to apologise for.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — these are Robinson’s words. What travels badly is when and to whom he said them, and how much of the answer gets left out.

items.who: “Said to his Brooklyn Dodgers teammates in 1947”
items.why: Simple English Wikiquote ↗ labels it “Statement to teammates on the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947,” citing The Impact and Legacy Years, 1941, 1947, 1968 (2000) by Fred Pulis, p. 100; Libquotes ↗ repeats the same framing but cites p. 20 of the same book. Robinson’s own account puts the words in 1954, addressed to an umpire — and in 1947 he was still keeping his promise to Branch Rickey not to answer back at all.

Goodreads ↗ prints the two sentences with no source whatever, under its own notice that “Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.” PassItOn ↗ credits only “Jackie Robinson, Major League Baseball player, civil rights activist.”

Reprints commonly punch the line up as “disliking me — all I ask…” (PassItOn ↗) or trail it off with an ellipsis, which is also how dozens of books indexed by Open Library ↗ carry it. In the source it is two flat declarative sentences, and it does not stop there.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Robinson, in his own book: a 1954 reply to an umpire, published in Baseball Has Done It (Lippincott, 1964) and cited to pp. 9–10 by Wikiquote ↗ — and the sentence everyone stops at is the first of eight.

context.heading: Why he was being asked at all
lead: Robinson had spent his first three seasons keeping a bargain. Before signing him, Branch Rickey had acted out the abuse to come and asked whether he could take it without fighting back. “I didn’t think I could,” Robinson remembered. “I didn’t see why I should.” He did it anyway — and then Rickey released him from it: “You’ve earned the right to be yourself, Jackie.”

What followed was a louder, sharper Robinson, and not everyone welcomed it. On a plane in 1954 an umpire who had known him since his 1946 season in the International League asked what had changed. The answer was not a plea to be liked. It was a refusal of the whole premise — and it ends, past the part that fits on a poster, with “I am not an Uncle Tom. I am in this fight to stay.”
detailsBody: Robinson published the exchange himself, ten years after it happened, in Baseball Has Done It — a book built mostly from his interviews with Black and Afro-Latino players about integration. The retort sits in the opening pages as a framing incident, not as an aphorism.

Because the record is Robinson’s own recollection rather than a contemporaneous transcript, the umpire is never named and the date is given only as 1954. That is as precise as the evidence goes; anything more specific circulating online is invention.
context.pull: I’m after something much more important than your favor or disfavor.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced Quotes section carries the full passage and cites it as Robinson responding circa 1954 to an umpire who had known him 8 years before and said "I liked you much better when you were less aggressive", as quoted in Baseball Has Done It (1964) by Robinson, pp. 9-10.

The Harvard Crimson's 1972 article reproduces the exchange verbatim: Robinson boarded a plane in 1954 with an umpire who had known him since 1946; the umpire asked "What's made you change your attitude, Jackie? I liked you much better when you were less aggressive"; Robinson replied "I'm not concerned with your liking or disliking me. All I ask is that you respect me as a human being..." ending "I am not an Uncle Tom. I am in this fight to stay." It also carries Rickey's "You've earned the right to be yourself, Jackie" and Robinson's "I didn't think I could. I didn't see why I should."

Open Library's full-text search returns the phrase "we believe our color is an asset. Your dislike of my aggressiveness" from inside two scanned copies of Baseball has done it by Jackie Robinson, confirming the book contains the passage.

Open Library's full-text search shows the phrase "All I ask is that you respect me as a human being" appearing in roughly 86 books, mostly secondary works quoting Robinson with an ellipsis and no source.
The Open Library edition record for Baseball has done it gives: Lippincott, Philadelphia, 1964, 216 pages, by statement "by Jackie Robinson ; edited by Charles Dexter", LCCN 64014467.

The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of Baseball has done it by Jackie Robinson (1919-1972); the item metadata records the scanned edition as the 2005 Ig Publishing reissue, ISBN 9780975251720.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame page records Jackie Robinson as inducted in 1962, a second baseman with the Brooklyn Dodgers 1947-1956, born 1919 and died 1972 in Stamford, Connecticut, and the player who broke baseball's color barrier.
Simple English Wikiquote presents the quote as a "Statement to teammates on the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947", citing The Impact and Legacy Years, 1941, 1947, 1968 (2000) by Fred Pulis, p. 100.

Libquotes presents the quote as a "Statement to teammates on the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947, as quoted in The Impact and Legacy Years, 1941, 1947, 1968 (2000) by Fred Pulis, p. 20", and gives Robinson's dates as born January 31, 1919 and died October 24, 1972.
Goodreads presents the two sentences with no source, under the notice "Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads."

PassItOn prints the quote with a dash instead of a full stop ("disliking me - all I ask...") and attributes it only to "Jackie Robinson, Major League Baseball player, civil rights activist", with no source.
A search of Quote Investigator for "respect me as a human being" returns no article about this quotation or about Jackie Robinson, confirming QI has not investigated this line.
